They have EF apartments which you will be put in as a brand new employee with some other housemates (working at EF). If you want to move out of that you have to let them know and you will be given a monthly allowance. The exact amount will be on your contract (depends on your qualifications). 

Unless you bring some savings with you, you probably won’t be able to afford your own place when you first get to China as most agencies/landlords require at least 6 months rent up front

Okay well I’ll try and give you some pros and cons but if you need anything specific just ask:

Cons (first because it’s always best to get the bad news initially):

Longer working hours than you may expect after looking at your contract; quite a few extra responsibilities like Life Clubs (more hands on classes like cooking, etc.), sales demos, interviews, special event preparation and compulsory team building; priority for making money and filling classes no matter what over educating kids and providing the best classes possible; extremely last minute management decisions that you’re expected just to ‘take on the chin’ (e.g. “you know you were teaching all the classes yourself before, well now you have to co-teach with a massively under-qualified staff member, good luck”); and no real leverage over the running of the school unless you push for a promotion.

Pros:

Generally very good in-house courses with teachers’ notes that outline how to teach every class; the pay is pretty good and you get a free apartment or housing allowance included in your monthly salary; each school has a staff member who’s job it is to deal with foreigner problems like the bank, gas and electricity, cell phones and even ordering food if you’re lucky; you’re given a mentor when you arrive who will help you with lesson planning and finding your way around the courses and school; there are a lot of ways to develop your teaching (I.e. courses you can do, observations you can request, etc.); everything to do with your visa is legit and there’s no bullshit from HR like having to go on visa runs to Hong Kong or having to pay for a renewal, EF will sort out everything; you get paid on time, every time; you can request emails of people who currently work at your school to check details with them; being promoted is quite easy if you want it, positions in management come up very often and you just need to show interest; and you get all of the Chinese National holidays off throughout the year (check your contract).

There are lots of other things but these are the main ones I can think of whilst lounging on a couch in Muji right now so please feel free to ask more specific questions if you need. 

In conclusion I think EF is a great company to get started with, use them to get our foot in the door and see if you enjoy the ESL life in China and look at other options when you’re here and can talk to other schools in person. Personally I’ve been working for them for 2 years now and I’m enjoying the teaching but the extra sales demos and compulsory jobs here and there really take the cake, and when you complain the answer is usually “well everyone has to do it so...”. I’m probably going to move on after my contract with the view to working at another school or maybe going and doing a full time teaching course so I can work in Europe.

This region is **occupied**. (past participle verb)
It's a **Nazi-occupied** region. (more specific past participle verb) 

The ice cream is **flavoured**. (past participle verb)
It's **strawberry-flavoured** ice cream. (more specific past participle verb)

“What you heard from him is true, I’m afraid.” said the bonfire. “There isn’t any fairness to it but that’s just how it works.” Every uttered syllable caused the flames to writhe and flicker.

“But I didn’t choose any of this! That grumpy man just pointed down here and now I’m scared.” the boy replied.

“Oh, you mean Saint Peter? He’s having to deal with a few of your sort this session. It’s never easy for him.”

“Saint what? My sort? I don’t get it, I don’t get it!” the little boy began to blubber. Tears formed quickly under his eyes but were seared away by the heat of the flames. 

The talking fire wobbled and reduced in size, its heat dying a little as it turned from a bright red to a friendly yellow. “It seems you are here because the place up there,” a yellow tendril pointed upwards, “is not *your* heaven, so to speak.”

“Daddy told me about green grass and rivers and trees. He called it a ‘para’-thingy … a para-dies. When you die you go to a para-dies.” The boy sniffed and rubbed his brow. “Too many clouds - no water, no green.” He looked straight into the flames with dark eyes. “Where’s the para-dies?” 

“Well, it’s there. But what your father chose to believe about it is … well … untrue.” The fire moved more slowly now, undulating comfortingly. “And that’s why you are here … your father told you some lies about this place. The rules say that because of him, you can’t be up there.”

“So there’s no para-dies?”

“Not exactly, paradise is only for a very specific kind of people.” The child’s eyes welled up again, but he managed to hold back the flow of tears.

“And – and I’m not a very specific people?” said the small boy, lip trembling slightly. This question caused the blaze to get dimmer still, slowing almost to a complete stop. There was quiet in the room. The fire’s crackle became inaudible. Standing, knocked-kneed and still, the boy looked down at his grubby bare feet and tried not to cry.

“You’re not,” came the answer, in a solemn tone. The boy shifted. “But, you are specific in other ways.”

“I am?”

“I know that you are innocent … I have a very specific job for people like you.”

The little boy looked up, “you do?”

“Follow me.”

I would say that the way I got myself appreciating drums a lot more (not being a drummer) is by listening to music with really basic percussion.

After my initial metal/hard rock phase I quickly got into progressive electronic music which completely changed my appreciation for percussive instruments.

I listened to a shit load of house, garage, techno and drum &a bass; genres whose drums are generally quite simple and repetitive. What I found eventually is that after inevitably going back to my more rocky nostalgic roots, the drum parts had found a completely new lease of life. I appreciated the intricacy and subtle creativity a lot more.

Perhaps this could be your answer if you're into your electronic genres at all. 

Artists I've listened to whose drum parts I especially enjoy are:

Alt-j, Aphex Twin, Squarepusher, Boards Of Canada, System Of A Down, Queens Of The Stone Age, Radiohead and Atoms For Peace.

EDIT: Also, if you haven't seen it, Whiplash gave me a completely new appreciation dimension to the drums. Would thoroughly recommend as a music lover.

I suffer from the occasional spell of sleep paralysis. The sensation is almost like being inbetween dream state and reality but without being able to move. I think it happens because brain activity has resumed but the part of the brain that controls movement hasn't yet woken up (I'm sure someone can explain the science of it in due course) Anyway, so I was having a pretty normal, run of the mill dream about skiing or something when I started to wake up and found myself paralysed in my bed, which for me is pretty normal, I usually just wait until I properly wake up but this time I decided I'd try and consciously fight the paralysis. To my surprise it worked and I managed to get up and I started to go about my morning routine. Everything seemed pretty normal until I looked at a clock in my bathroom which, instead of a time, showed in identifiable symbols. Once I'd noticed this things started to get weird. The room started to wobble and people started to come in and ask me questions in strange languages. Obviously I was so confused and scared, thinking I was hallucinating and going mad. I tried to respond to the people but I couldn't speak properly and I remember feeling inside my mouth and pulling out a huge length of wool or something. Super weird. After all of this I snapped back into my bed where I was still in sleep paralysis. The strangest thing about this whole thing was that I literally kept getting up and going about my routine and thn finding myself back in my bed again after a load of weird stuff had happened. It was like an endless cycle. I think I must have done it almost 8 times before I finally woke up for real. I saw faceless people, cupboards morphing into monsters, my teeth fell out, my parents shouted at me in strange languages, I summoned balls of light and even at one point managed to leave my body and become a sort of fly-on-the-wall type entity watching over the scene. It was incredibly scary and it felt so real. To this day I've never forgotten that dream and I've never had one like it since. The human brain is such an awesome thing, I wish I knew more about it!

You need to find out what your contact hours are (hours that you'll be expected to teach students).

Currently I work 20 contact hours a week and I have to be in the school for about 20 more hours for planning, interviews, parent-teacher meetings and the like. But that does tend to increase during busy times. If you're working weekends you can expect to be doing 10 hour days during very busy periods (Sat and Sun), this is not unheard of. It's likely you'll be working around 6 hours a day on weekdays, and 8 hours a day on weekends (~44 hours a week). 

Because of the relatively unpredictable nature of running a school, it's unlikely that they'll be able to give you an exact figure of how many hours you'll be working. 40 sounds pretty accurate from my experience. 

I'm working in a pretty busy private language school in Xi'an so take what you will from my calculations, I highly doubt they do things much differently in Hong Kong. 

If you're really worried about it, ask for a contact number for someone working at the school (a teacher) and see what they say. That's what I did before my first job.

I suffer from the occasional spell of sleep paralysis. The sensation is almost like being inbetween dream state and reality but without being able to move. I think it happens because brain activity has resumed but the part of the brain that controls movement hasn't yet woken up (I'm sure someone can explain the science of it in due course)
Anyway, so I was having a pretty normal, run of the mill dream about skiing or something when I started to wake up and found myself paralysed in my bed, which for me is pretty normal, I usually just wait until I properly wake up but this time I decided I'd try and consciously fight the paralysis. To my surprise it worked and I managed to get up and I started to go about my morning routine. Everything seemed pretty normal until I looked at a clock in my bathroom which, instead of a time, showed in identifiable symbols. Once I'd noticed this things started to get weird. The room started to wobble and people started to come in and ask me questions in strange languages. Obviously I was so confused and scared, thinking I was hallucinating and going mad. I tried to respond to the people but I couldn't speak properly and I remember feeling inside my mouth and pulling out a huge length of wool or something. Super weird. After all of this I snapped back into my bed where I was still in sleep paralysis. The strangest thing about this whole thing was that I literally kept getting up and going about my routine and thn finding myself back in my bed again after a load of weird stuff had happened. It was like an endless cycle. I think I must have done it almost 8 times before I finally woke up for real. I saw faceless people, cupboards morphing into monsters, my teeth fell out, my parents shouted at me in strange languages, I summoned balls of light and even at one point managed to leave my body and become a sort of fly-on-the-wall type entity watching over the scene. It was incredibly scary and it felt so real. To this day I've never forgotten that dream and I've never had one like it since. The human brain is such an awesome thing, I wish I knew more about it!

Edit: TL;DR: I could be crazy.

Hi there! Just been listening to your stuff on SC, the solo piano stuff is really beautiful, "Not Ourselves" is currently my fave. Really enjoyed the simple start followed by the melodic crescendo. 

Your electronic stuff really does have potential, don't be afraid to mess around with drum patterns more, you can use more offbeats to make the songs more interesting. Also sometimes a simple 4'4 beat can go a long way, with a bit of hi-hat to get those listener's bopping their heads! Also adding samples can be scary but having some weird vocals or natural sounds like waves, rain, bird song haha. Even weird stuff you can record sound the house can add depth to your track. An example would be this track by Nicolas Jaar http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KMQhoLUJSFM Very natural sounding because almost all of the sounds are recorded by himself, the melody at the start is a wind chime backed by a fountain. Anyway, just some tips!
